units.translation: unshaken, from στέμβω [to shake constantly], which means to move continuously, which Aeschylus mentions.
Indeed, groans are the healers of toils.
I sigh, I groan, I wail.
Row, row, and groan for my sake.
I lament the present and the coming calamity.
As a substantive, τὸ στενόν [the narrow place] means narrows.
And when the multitude of ships was gathered in the narrows.
affording a narrow passage or transit.
at the very narrow-passaged gates of the lake.
i.e. it is beneficial to be wise when constrained by narrow circumstances, as Hermann interprets it.
Homer used the Ionic form στεῖνος [narrowness], meaning a narrow way. The scholiast wrongly took the verb στένει [it groans] at Pr. 432 as the dative of the noun στένος [narrowness].
It is beneficial to be wise under narrowness.
it lies near the narrows of the sea.

In Ma first hand ὑποστένω [I groan under], from the second hand ὑπερστένω [I groan over], which Schuetz wrote separately ὕπερ στένω [I groan over], as at 68 τῶν Διός τ᾽ ἐχθρῶν ὕπερ | στένεις [you groan over the enemies of Zeus], although these examples differ in that in the latter the preposition, having undergone anastrophe, is placed in the sixth foot of the trimeter according to custom, while in the former it is in the fourth foot, although it could have been written σῶν στένω πόνων ὕπερ [I groan over your toils].
where ᾷ [with a shout] and στένει [it groans] are verbs, not nouns, as the scholiast believed, who wrote τῇ βοῇ [with the shout] and ἀπ᾿ εὐθείας τῆς τὸ στένος [from the nominative 'τὸ στένος'].
The sea wave cries out as it crashes together, the deep groans (thus from the copy for βαθύς [deep]).
the towers groan, the man-loving earth groans.
so that the city of the Persians groans.
it groans, the ground is struck and furrowed.
the ancient city of Priam, much-lamenting, groans greatly.
even if you groan in your troubles, nevertheless.
and those who speak well of the man groan.
Why do they not groan, not having obtained a portion of the day?
looking at the wealth of others, he groans.
I groan for your accursed fortune.
groaning for your honor and that of your kinsmen.
such a misfortune, in addition to the former one, is yours to groan over.
the whole city groans for its emptiness of men.
I weep then, groaning for the misfortune of this house.
Let us groan then for the double misfortune of these too.
for whom all the Asian land, having nurtured them, groans with fierce longing.
you groan over the enemies of Zeus
